Client kickoff meeting agenda for freelancers: a 30-minute call, minute by minute

2026-11-24

The contract is signed, the deposit is in and the client is keen to get going. It's tempting to skip the kickoff call and start work. But it's far easier to find out in a 30-minute call now than in week three that the client's content won't be ready, or that someone else will want to approve the final version.

This article gives you a client kickoff meeting agenda built for one freelancer and one client (or a small client team), not a twelve-person agency project. You'll get:

  • what to do in the day before the call
  • a 30-minute agenda you can copy, with timings
  • a line or two to say in each block
  • how to handle new ideas that come up on the call
  • a recap email to send afterwards

Not legal advice. The agenda and recap email help you and your client agree how the project will run. They aren't a contract and don't replace one. Payment terms, ownership, liability and cancellation belong in a contract, ideally one reviewed by a qualified lawyer where you work.

What a kickoff call is for (and what it isn't)

By the time you get to kickoff, you should already have agreed the scope. Ideally that means a short written scope summary the client has confirmed. If you haven't got there yet, the client onboarding checklist walks through the steps from the first conversation to this point.

So kickoff isn't for negotiating the project. It has three narrower jobs:

  1. Check you both picture the same finished project. Reading the scope aloud, together, surfaces mismatches that a quick skim of a document doesn't.
  2. Turn the client's tasks into dates and names. "We'll send the photos" becomes "Priya sends the photos by the 3rd".
  3. Explain how feedback and changes will work, before anyone needs them. It's much easier to describe the process when nothing is at stake.

If the call starts turning into a new negotiation, that's a useful signal too. It usually means the scope wasn't as settled as it looked, and it's better to find that out now.

The day before the call

A little preparation makes the call shorter and calmer:

  • Send the scope summary again, with a one-line note: "We'll walk through this together tomorrow. No need to prepare anything."
  • Ask who's coming. "Will anyone else from your side join? It's helpful to have whoever approves the final version there, even for the first ten minutes."
  • List the client's tasks (content, access, logins, brand files, sign-offs) with the dates you need them. You'll confirm these on the call.
  • Open a blank notes page using the template further down, so you're writing in the same structure as the recap email.

The agenda (copy and paste)

Paste this into the calendar invite or the top of the welcome email. Change the timings to suit. If you only have 20 minutes, shorten blocks 2 and 5 rather than dropping block 3.

KICKOFF: [PROJECT NAME]
[DATE, TIME, TIME ZONE] · 30 minutes · [VIDEO LINK OR PHONE]
Attending: [YOUR NAME], [CLIENT NAMES AND ROLES]

1. Hello and roles (0:00-0:03)
   Who's here, who sends feedback, who gives the final yes.

2. The project on one page (0:03-0:10)
   Goal, deliverables, what "finished" means for each,
   and what isn't part of this project.

3. Your part and the dates (0:10-0:17)
   Content, access and decisions we need from you:
   who on your side owns each one, and by when.

4. Feedback and approval (0:17-0:22)
   How drafts arrive, how feedback comes back,
   how many rounds, how long each round takes.

5. When something new comes up (0:22-0:26)
   How we'll handle new ideas and changes.

6. Questions and next steps (0:26-0:30)
   Open questions, the first milestone,
   when the written recap will arrive.

What to cover in each block (and what to say)

1. Hello and roles (3 minutes)

Keep the introductions short and get to the roles quickly. The question that matters most:

"Just so I know who to send things to: who will put feedback together on drafts, and who gives the final yes?"

If those are two different people, write both names down. If the final approver isn't on the call, ask whether they could see the first draft early. A new opinion arriving at the final review can push a project late, and it's much easier to plan for once you know it's coming.

2. The project on one page (7 minutes)

Put the scope summary on screen so you're both looking at the same words, and read the goal line out loud. Then go through each deliverable and its "done when".

"For the homepage, 'done' means it's live on your site with your final text in place. Does that match what you were expecting?"

Then read the "not included" list, in a neutral tone:

"And just so it's clear, the online shop isn't part of this project. Happy to quote it separately later."

You're not looking for agreement on every word. You're listening for a pause or a "hmm, I thought…". If you hear one, note it and agree to follow up in writing. Don't rewrite the scope live on the call.

3. Your part and the dates (7 minutes)

This is the block most worth protecting. Go through each client task one at a time, and get a name and a date for each:

"I'll need the product photos by the 3rd to keep the first draft on schedule. Who on your side will send those?"

Wait for an actual answer, not a general "yes, we'll sort that out". If the date doesn't work for them, now is the time to move it, along with anything that depends on it. A task without an owner tends to become a delay without an explanation.

4. Feedback and approval (5 minutes)

Explain how a round works in plain terms:

"When I send a draft, please collect everyone's comments into one list and send it within three working days. That counts as one round. The project includes two rounds per page."

If you haven't settled on a number, the guide on how many revisions to include covers how to choose one and how to word it.

5. When something new comes up (4 minutes)

New ideas are normal, and saying so up front keeps them from becoming awkward later. One or two sentences is enough:

"If you think of something new along the way, send it over. I'll let you know whether it's covered by what we've agreed. If it isn't, you'll get a quick note with what it would cost and how it affects the dates, and you decide. Nothing extra starts without your OK."

If the client brings up a new idea during the call itself, don't put a price on it or say yes there and then. Add it to an "ideas" list in your notes, say "That's worth looking at. I'll write to you about it after the call", and move on. The out-of-scope request email guide has replies for when you follow up.

6. Questions and next steps (4 minutes)

Ask "What haven't we covered that's on your mind?", then confirm three things out loud: the first milestone and its date, the client's first task and its date, and when your recap email will arrive.

A notes template for the call

Use the same headings as the recap email so writing it afterwards takes a few minutes:

KICKOFF NOTES: [PROJECT] · [DATE]
Attending:
Feedback from:            Final approval:
Scope: matches / questions raised:
Client tasks (item / owner / date):
Feedback: rounds ___ · reply window ___ working days
New ideas raised (not agreed):
First milestone + date:
Anything that changed:

The recap email (send within one working day)

The call isn't the record. The email is. Send it while the conversation is fresh, and ask for a reply so you know it's been read.

Subject: [Project name]: what we agreed at kickoff

Hi [Name],

Thanks for the call today. Here's what we agreed, so we're both working from the same notes.

Who's who: [Name] sends combined feedback; [Name] gives final approval.

Scope: no changes to the summary you confirmed on [date]. (Or: one change, [describe it]. I'll send an updated summary for you to confirm.)

What I need from you:

  • [Item], from [owner], by [date]
  • [Item], from [owner], by [date]

Feedback: [number] rounds per [deliverable]. Each round, please gather everyone's comments into a single reply and send it within [number] working days.

Ideas we noted: [idea]. This isn't in the current project. I'll come back to you with options by [date].

Next: [first milestone] on [date].

If I've got anything wrong, just reply and let me know. Otherwise, could you reply with a quick "looks right"?

[Your name]

Listing the ideas you noted, with a date you'll follow up by, matters more than it might seem. It shows the client their idea was heard, and it puts in writing that the idea isn't part of the current work.

When the call doesn't go to plan

  • The approver didn't show up. Run the call anyway. In the recap, add: "As [approver] wasn't on the call, could you forward this to them? It would help to hear if they see anything differently."
  • The client wants to change the scope. Note it, don't agree on the call, and follow up with an updated scope summary and any price or date change for them to confirm.
  • A client task has no date. Suggest one in the recap ("I've put the 5th; let me know if that doesn't work"), rather than leaving it open.
  • The client prefers not to have a call. Send the agenda as an email with a question under each heading, and treat their written reply as the recap. You'll lose some of the tone you'd pick up live, but you'll still have the answers in writing.

Where kickoff sits

Kickoff comes after the intake questionnaire, the quote, the confirmed scope summary and the contract. It comes before the first piece of work. The client onboarding checklist has every step on one page, including a compact version of a kickoff agenda.
